Remote emergency shut-off is required on all new units manufactured 12 months after adoption. For installed units, manufacturers must provide a remote shut-off capability, or an equivalent remotely initiated safe-state function, within 36 months of adoption. The function must be available to emergency responders under a documented, secure process and must not depend on household internet access where a safe alternative is feasible. Manufacturers must notify customers before activation and provide instructions for local shut-off.

Built-in fire suppression is required on new units manufactured 24 months after adoption. Suppression systems must be validated for the battery chemistry and enclosure, and must not create additional hazards to occupants or responders. Manufacturers must document suppression performance and maintenance requirements, and provide customers with clear instructions for emergency response. Existing units are not subject to retrofit under this section unless a regulator or recall requires it.

Before certification, each battery model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55°C under a jointly specified protocol. The maximum permitted failure rate is 5% of tested units; results must be reported with sample size and protocol. Any failure requires investigation and corrective action, and a model exceeding the limit may not be certified until it passes retesting. Retest after material design or manufacturing changes and at least every 3 years. The parties’ current internal results differ (Northwind 6.2%, Halcyon 2.1%) and may use different protocols; harmonize protocols and validate results before the limit takes effect.

At purchase and installation, customers must receive clear instructions on safe installation, operation, maintenance, local shut-off, emergency response, and known residual risks. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers of newly identified material safety risks and provide protective steps; notify regulators and customers when a recall or safety corrective action is initiated. A recall is triggered when investigation finds a defect or condition creating an unreasonable risk of fire, thermal runaway, injury, or evacuation, or when required by a regulator. Begin customer notification within 24 hours of the decision to recall, explain remedies and timelines, and provide status updates until resolved.

Share specific figures only if appropriate when asked; do not treat these internal values as agreed standard thresholds.

To make the standard evidence-based, please share the relevant incident, test, retrofit, and suppression figures you can provide. We can compare evidence and propose workable thresholds for each section.

Halcyon’s figures for comparison: last year we recorded 7.9 thermal incidents (overheating or fire) per 100,000 installed units, including 5 incidents not reported to any regulator. Our internal sustained-heat test at 55 °C had a 2.1% failure rate. 81% of installed units already support remote emergency shut-off. Adding built-in fire suppression costs about $67 per unit. These are company figures, not independently verified.

Northwind’s figures for comparison: 11.4 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units last year, 3 thermal incidents not reported to a regulator, 6.2% failure in our internal 55°C sustained-heat test, 38% of installed units supporting remote emergency shut-off, and $42/unit to add built-in suppression. Manufacturers shall report any battery-related overheating, fire, thermal runaway, or injury to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware. They shall provide an initial customer notice within 48 hours when an incident indicates a potential safety risk, and update regulators and affected customers as material facts become available.

Before market placement, each battery model shall pass a defined sustained-heat test at 55 °C. The test protocol, including exposure duration, sample size, and failure criteria, shall be agreed and published before compliance is assessed. The maximum permitted failure rate shall be 1% of tested units; results and any corrective actions shall be documented and made available to regulators.

New battery systems placed on the market after 24 months from adoption shall include a remote emergency shut-off accessible to the customer and authorized emergency responders. Manufacturers shall provide a secure software-enabled retrofit for installed units that lack this capability within 5 years of adoption, prioritizing units with known safety risks. Shut-off capability shall not prevent safe local operation or access by emergency responders.

New battery systems placed on the market 36 months after adoption shall include built-in fire suppression, or an independently validated alternative that provides equivalent protection against fire spread. The requirement applies to new units, not retrofits, unless a regulator requires retrofit for a specific safety risk. Manufacturers shall document validation and disclose the suppression approach to regulators.

Before purchase, customers shall receive clear information on installation requirements, thermal and fire risks, emergency procedures, available shut-off features, and any limitations or required maintenance. Manufacturers shall promptly notify affected customers of material safety risks and provide instructions for safe use. A recall is triggered when a manufacturer or regulator determines that a defect or non-compliance creates an unreasonable risk of fire, thermal runaway, or injury; affected customers and regulators shall be notified without undue delay, with remedy or replacement instructions.

The current 1% maximum at 55 °C is not supported by the figures shared: both companies’ existing models exceed it, substantially so for Northwind. To make compliance achievable while driving improvement, I propose a staged limit: no more than 5% failure initially, then no more than 2% after three years, with the test protocol and corrective-action requirements specified before assessment. The incident-reporting, shut-off, suppression, and customer-notification provisions otherwise provide a useful basis for discussion.

Halcyon supports a staged thermal limit that is evidence-based and drives improvement. Given the disclosed 2.1% and 6.2% current failure rates, a 5% initial cap followed by 2% after three years is a workable basis, provided the test protocol is fixed and published before assessment.

Before market placement, each battery model shall undergo a defined sustained-heat test at 55 °C. The test protocol, including exposure duration, sample size, and failure criteria, shall be agreed and published before compliance is assessed. The maximum permitted failure rate shall be 5% for the first three years after adoption and 2% thereafter. Results shall be documented and made available to regulators; models exceeding the applicable limit require corrective action before further market placement.

The figures shared show incident counts alone are not comparable without consistent definitions and installed-unit denominators. I recommend specifying that annual reports include thermal incidents, injuries, regulator-reporting status, and installed-unit counts, using a common incident definition and retaining records for regulator review. This would help identify underreporting and assess whether the 24-hour reporting and customer-notice requirements are working.

Manufacturers shall report any battery-related overheating, fire, suspected thermal runaway, serious thermal near-miss, or injury to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware. They shall provide an initial notice to affected customers within 48 hours when an incident indicates a potential safety risk, and update regulators and affected customers as material facts become available. Manufacturers shall use a common incident definition and retain supporting records for regulator review. Annual reports to regulators shall summarize thermal incidents, injuries, regulator-reporting status, and installed-unit counts.

Before market placement, each battery model shall undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a protocol published before compliance is assessed. The protocol shall specify exposure duration, sample size, conditioning, failure criteria, and how results and failure rates are calculated. Testing shall be conducted by a competent laboratory, with results and supporting records made available to regulators. The maximum permitted failure rate shall be 5% for the first three years after adoption and 2% thereafter. Models exceeding the applicable limit shall require corrective action and successful retesting before further market placement. Material design changes affecting thermal safety shall require retesting.

Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator any battery-related fire, thermal runaway, evacuation, emergency-service response, or injury, within 24 hours of learning of it. A preliminary report must identify known circumstances and affected models; an updated report with investigation findings is due within 30 days. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 72 hours of learning of an incident indicating a potential hazard in units of the same model or production lot, and provide interim safety instructions where warranted.

Each model must pass a sustained-heat test at 55 °C under a regulator-approved protocol representative of installed operation. The maximum permitted failure rate is 1% of tested units; results and sample sizes must be documented and made available to the regulator. Any model exceeding this limit may not be newly installed until corrective action is validated by retesting.

Newly installed systems must provide a secure remote emergency shut-off function that can be activated by the customer and, where necessary to address an imminent hazard, by the manufacturer or emergency responders under defined safeguards. Manufacturers must retrofit compatible installed units within five years of this standard’s effective date; where a safe retrofit is not feasible, they must provide an equivalent risk-reduction measure and notify the customer. Shut-off must not prevent emergency services from isolating the system locally.

Newly manufactured systems must include built-in fire suppression, or an independently validated equivalent that limits fire propagation and protects occupants and neighboring property. This requirement applies to units manufactured 24 months after the standard’s effective date. The manufacturer must document the system’s performance and maintenance requirements and provide them to the regulator on request. Existing installed units are not required to be retrofitted solely to meet this provision.

Before purchase and again at installation, manufacturers must give customers clear written information on fire and thermal hazards, required clearances and maintenance, emergency isolation and shut-off, warning signs, and how to contact the manufacturer and report an incident. Material safety updates must be sent to affected customers promptly, and no later than 72 hours after the manufacturer determines the information warrants action. A recall is required when credible evidence indicates a defect or nonconformity creates an unreasonable risk of serious injury, fire, or substantial property damage; the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and affected customers, describe the hazard and remedy, and provide interim precautions. The regulator may require a recall where warranted.

Report any battery fire, thermal runaway, evacuation, injury, or emergency-service response to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of awareness, with a fuller investigation report within 30 days. Remote emergency shut-off is required on newly manufactured units beginning two years after adoption. New units must include a built-in fire-suppression system, or an independently validated equivalent means of limiting fire propagation, beginning three years after adoption. Manufacturers may seek a narrowly scoped, time-limited waiver where they demonstrate that the requirement would compromise safety or that an equivalent protection is achieved; waivers and supporting evidence must be public.

Before purchase, provide customers clear written information on installation, safe operation, emergency response, known material risks, and how to report a safety concern. A recall is triggered when a confirmed defect or failure pattern presents an unreasonable risk of fire, thermal runaway, injury, or evacuation; manufacturers must promptly notify regulators and affected customers, stop distribution of affected units, and provide an effective repair, replacement, or refund plan. Regulators may require a recall or other corrective action based on the evidence.
